tasks.task: Search for the differences between "fewer" and "less" in grammar section, and provide examples illustrating their correct usage from the Cambridge Dictionary.

With 'of', we say 'less of' before singular nouns and 'fewer of' before plural nouns. Examples from the Cambridge Dictionary grammar page: I do less work at weekends than I used to. / Better cycle routes would mean fewer cars and fewer accidents. / It was funny to begin with, but as time went on, it became less of a joke. / Every year in Britain about 5,000 people die on the roads. Fewer are killed at work. / We need fewer staff in the office now, but more in the shops at peak times.

tasks.task: Use the Cambridge Dictionary to understand the rules for forming and using comparative and superlative adjectives in English Grammar, including example sentences.
tasks.answer: Used the Cambridge Dictionary British Grammar article 'Comparison: adjectives (bigger, biggest, more interesting)' (https://dictionary.cambridge.org/grammar/british-grammar/comparison-adjectives-bigger-biggest-more-interesting, under Grammar > Adjectives and adverbs > Adjectives > Comparative and superlative adjectives). Rules learned: (1) Comparative adjectives compare one person/thing with another and are normally followed by 'than'; superlative adjectives compare one person/thing with the whole group. (2) One-syllable adjectives form comparatives/superlatives with -er/-est (tall-taller-tallest, old-older-oldest), with spelling rules such as consonant doubling (big-bigger-biggest) and -e endings (nice-nicer-nicest). (3) Two-syllable adjectives may take -er/-est or more/most; longer adjectives use more/most (more interesting, the most frightening), and less/least express lower degree. (4) Irregular forms include good-better-best and bad-worse-worst. (5) Usage: much/a lot/far + comparative; 'the -er, the -er' and 'the more, the more' constructions; 'the' with superlatives; prepositions after superlatives. Example sentences from the article (85 extracted, saved to final_runs/run_004/extracted_examples.txt): 'Josh is taller than his sister.'; 'Joe's older than Mike. (comparing one person with another)'; 'Sheila is the youngest girl in the family. (comparing one person with the whole group she belongs to)'; 'I'm more interested in music than sport.'; 'The most frightening film I've ever seen was Alfred Hitchcock's Psycho.'; 'What is the least expensive way of travelling in Japan?'

tasks.task: Use Cambridge Dictionary to understand the use of articles ('a', 'an', 'the') in English Grammar, including examples of usage with both countable and uncountable nouns.
tasks.answer: Cambridge Dictionary Grammar page 'A/an and the' (https://dictionary.cambridge.org/grammar/british-grammar/a-an-and-the) explains English articles. A/an and the are articles (determiners) that go before a noun. Indefinite articles: 'a/an' show the noun is not already known to speaker/listener (e.g., 'Do you have a car?', 'No, actually, I live in an apartment.'). Definite article: 'the' shows the noun is already known and makes it specific (e.g., 'Where did we park the car?', 'Have you been to the ice rink?'). Countable nouns: a/an is used only with singular countable nouns ('I have a sister and a brother.', 'That was an excellent meal.'); 'the' works with singular and plural countable nouns ('The lion roared.', 'The lions roared.'). Uncountable nouns: a/an is NOT used before uncountable nouns ('Could I have rice instead of potatoes with my fish?', 'I hope we have nice weather.'); 'the' can be used before uncountable nouns when referring to a specific example ('The rice we bought in the Thai shop is much better than the supermarket rice.', 'The weather was awful last summer.'); quantities use expressions like a bit of / a piece of / a litre of ('That’s an amazing bit of news.', 'Could I have a litre of milk, please?').
